lead_html:
MARVIN keeps Claude Code working between sessions by remembering context, applying the right skill for each task, and submitting changes for review. Rather than dumping the entire conversation history into every session, MARVIN loads just the context a task needs.

Deployed on two Macs (a primary automation host running continuous background agents, and a laptop where daily work happens), MARVIN synchronizes code and work state between machines so a session can resume from either one.

sections.heading: The dashboard
sections.body_html:
Seven tabs organize the work:

  • Metrics — tokens spent by model and by task type, usage trending against the monthly API budget.
  • Workshop — every ticket, PR, and proposal sorted by whose move it is (Now · Projects · Shipped · Proposals). Merges, activity and pipeline health are shown here too.
  • MR Review — pending pull requests with side-by-side diffs and inline comments.
  • Health — machine status (CPU, memory, disk, thermal), background agent health (daily digest, research colony, code sync, auto-fixer), and circuit breaker counts.
  • Docs — a live view of the design docs, decisions (ADRs) and planning files.
  • Activity — event log of everything the system did: skill runs, ticket dispatch, failed runs (with causes), and health alerts.
  • Portfolio — a manager for project pages, showing current content, flagging staleness and providing one-click authoring and deployment.

Each tab is Electron-based for speed and native integration with the system; most tabs pull live data from either the same machine or the other Mac over SSH.

sections.heading: The pipeline
sections.body_html:
Issues labelled ready-for-agent flow through an automated dispatch system:

  1. An agent claims the ticket in an isolated worktree and plans the work (asking for clarification when the brief is ambiguous).
  2. A second agent executes the plan, writing code or prose.
  3. Both the plan and the changes are tested: the repo's own test suite (pytest, vitest) runs to check for regressions, and specialized checks verify the specific task (e.g., architecture review for refactors, privacy scan for user-facing content).
  4. If the tests pass or improve, a pull request is raised with the plan and evidence attached.
  5. You review the PR in the dashboard and approve or send it back.
  6. The merge gate rebases, re-runs tests, installs dependencies, and merges.

Every failure is recorded with its cause. If the same failure repeats on three different tickets, the circuit breaker pauses dispatch and alerts you, preventing a cascade of identical mistakes.

sections.heading: Memory and routing
sections.body_html:
At the start of each session, MARVIN narrows the full codebase down to just what this task needs:

  • A tag manifest maps each of the 34 installed skills to their relevant code areas, so a session looking for "architecture" loads the right skills.
  • Vector search (768-dim embeddings of the memory and codebase) finds the most relevant earlier memories and patterns.
  • Keyword re-ranking (BM25) boosts results that match multiple query terms.
  • Only the top results are loaded as context.

This approach cuts the typical context from thousands of lines down to hundreds, so a small model (Haiku) can often do the work of a larger one — real measurements from the bench show Haiku handles recall and routing at ~60% of Sonnet's cost.

sections.heading: Phone and voice (beta)
sections.body_html:
MARVIN Mobile (iOS, private beta) brings MARVIN to iPhone and iPad as a companion app. Sessions start on the phone, dispatch work to the Mac, and display results live. Work-in-progress features include device identity and Face ID gating, offline support via foundation models, and proactive delivery of important alerts.

MARVIN Voice (macOS, private beta) adds voice I/O as one of three interaction modes: speak a request, type it, or use the web dashboard. The voice endpoint chains speech recognition, intent routing, and dispatch in one round trip, so "hey MARVIN, review my PR" dispatches the right task immediately.

sections.heading: The system behind it
sections.body_html:
Three main pieces work together:

  • The engine (this repo) contains the pipeline logic, skills, templates, and all dashboards and analysis tools.
  • Shared state (memory, settings, backlogs) is synced between machines: code via git, runtime state via SSH and databases.
  • Background agents run on the primary Mac mini: a daily digest generator, a research colony that tracks AI papers, health checks, code sync and auto-fixing of safe issues.

Both machines share a single Tailscale network, so they reach each other and external services over encrypted, identity-verified links. Code changes are synced every 30 minutes; work state (database snapshots, task logs) syncs per-job.

sections.heading: What it costs
sections.body_html:
The system tracks every Claude API call: which model, which task, tokens in and out, success or failure. Every "this is better" claim about efficiency is backed by a number from the bench.

Real example (October 2026): a routing query asking "what were the bench results last session?" was answered by Haiku (retrieval from ChromaDB) at 60% of what Sonnet would have cost, with zero accuracy loss because the memory had the answer. Scaling to hundreds of queries a session, that one optimization saves ~40% of tokens month-to-month on medium-token tasks.

The system runs on a home machine (a Mac mini), not cloud infrastructure, so the only recurring costs are the Claude API calls and internet. This keeps both latency and cost low for a 24/7 background system.
